Has the government any information as to the destruction of the papers connected with the Stanstead by-election of January, 1908. I have a telegram informing me that when the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery was summoned to produce the election papers in order to prove the holding of the election and the status of the petitioners, he declared on oath that the papers in the box labelled ' By-election of Stanstead, January 19, 1908,' were the papers of the general election of 1904, and that apparently the papers of the by-election had been destroyed. Has the government information on the subject ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes. This matter was called to my attention a week ago last Friday by Mr. Foley, the present Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. Mr. Lamothe, the former Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, died at the end of March and Mr. Foley, the assistant clerk, was appointed to the vacancy about the 20th of April. About a week afterwards he came to my office and informed me that he had been summoned as a witness to appear in the Stanstead election case at Sherbrooke and that he could not find the papers connected with the election. He was accompanied by Mr. Chad-Mr. J, D. REID,
wick, a clerk in the Privy Council, who had been transferred and had been acting as assistant to Mr. Lamonthe in his office. I may say that the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is in this building and Mr. Foley was nominally assistant clerk of the Crown in Chancery, but he had his office in the Privy Council Department and acted only when the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery was absent. We appointed Mr. Foley to the office in accordance with the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission, which I think will commend itself to the judgment of the House and which certainly jommmended itself to our judgment. We transferred the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery from the Privy Council to the staff of the House of Commons. When Mr. Foley informed me he could not find the papers I told him the only thing to do was to make further search and if he could not find them to attend the court and state the particulars. I advised him at the same time to report to Mr. Speaker the fact that he could not find these papers. I may say, in justice to Mr. Lamothe, that all those who knew him in his lifetime will bear testimony that he was a most honourable, conscientious and painstaking officer.
I entirely concur in what the Prime Minister has said about Mr. Lamothe.

speechtext: I would like to repeat the question which I asked yesterday respecting the resignation or the supposed resignation of the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

maintopic: THE DEPUTY MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
The best way to answer the question which my hon. friend put yesterday is to read a letter from Colonel Gourdeau, which is as follows :
Department of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa, Canada, March 31, 1908.
Dear Mr. Brodeur,-I have worried every moment since the publication of the Civil Ser-vince Commissioners' Report containing accusations against the officials of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, which I feel are both unjust and untrue. I am convinced that a full and complete investigation will establish this and will clear the public mind of all the insinuations and reflections that have been made against them. As my presence in the department as deputy head might in some quarters be considered as prejudicial to the fullest inquiry, I beg to renew for the third time, my application for six months' leave of absence preparatory to superannuation and which you have so loyally hitherto refused to entertain under similar circumstances. I court the most rigid examination of all the department's transactions so far as I am concerned and by placing myself in your hands I hope to assist you in that regard. Again thanking you for the many kindnesses

which you have shown me as Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Believe me, yours very faithfully, (Sgd.) F. GOURDEAU.

House resumed adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Aylesworth for the second reading of Bill (No. 115) to amend the Dominion Elections Act and the proposed amendment of Mr. Roche (Marquette) thereto.

Mr. Speaker, when I moved the ad-jounment of the debate last night, I was referring to the election law which was formerly in operation in the province of Manitoba. I stated that it was nearer to my idea of what an election law should be than possibly any other law that had ever before been on the statute-books of this country. I made that statement because the law at that time was entirely free from partisan control or manipulation. That is the law that was in operation when the lists were revised in 1903, and that was the law that our friends opposite, particularly those from the province of Manitoba, paraded before this House and this country as being a good and proper law. Under that law certain Liberal officials were appointed in
connection with the preparation of the voters' lists. The law to-day is entirely different. Our Conservative friends who are in control of affairs in the province of Manitoba were not prepared to stand by that fair and honest and non-partisan preparation of the voters' lists. They only stood for it in one revision; that was for the list referred to by the Hon. Mr. Mickle as the cleanest list ever made in the province of Manitoba. The preparation of that list was entirely under the judges, and was free from any manipulationn by political partisans. I will read from the official ' Gazette ' of the province of Manitoba a notice to show that the board of judges had entire control of the situation :
Public notice is hereby given that the board of registration constituted to make and revise a new list of electors for the several electoral divisions of the province, has selected D. M. Walker, county court judge as chairman, and for the purposes of registration of electors, divided the several electoral divisions into registration districts, naming a registration clerk for each district. Following are the boundaries and limits of the several registration districts, with the name and post office address of the registration clerk.
That is followed by a proclamation in which practically the same words are used:
Notice is hereby given that the board of registration constituted to make and revise a uew list of electors for the several electoral divisions of the province have made the following additions, alterations and corrections in the boundaries and limits of certain of. the registration districts and in the list of registration clerks.
Further on, there is this notice with regard to the appointment of revising barristers to revise the list:
Whereas, it has been determined to make and revise a new list of electors in and for the several electoral divisions of the province pursuant to the provisions of 'The Manitoba Elections Act.'	. .
And, whereas, pursuant to the profusions of sections 70 and 71 of the said Act, the chairman of >the board of registration has intimated to the provincial secretary the appointment of revising officers for the several electoral divisions.
That is the law about which our hon. friends are pleased to talk and say it is so fair and just. They have tried to mislead the people by these statements, have tried to make them believe that that law is under operation to-day and that the judges still have full control^ over the preparation and revision of the lists.
No one ever tried to do any such thing as that.

I beg your pardon, I have seen it in print and I have heard it repeated, not by my hon. friend it is true, but he is not the only man in this country and has not control of everything. What

was done in regard to the preparation of voters' lists, what treatment was meted out to the people of Manitoba at that time by the judges who had control of the situation ?-I shall refer only to a couple of constituencies with which I am personally acquainted. I find that the judges then gave ample time for registration and revision. In the local division from which I come they established sixteen registration places appointing a registration clerk for each of these sixteen registration places. These registration clerks had to receive applications there for one whole week, from Monday morning May 25, until Saturday night May 30, and the hours were from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m., giving ample time for the people to register. They were not confined to a couple of hours, as has been the case in the last few years, or to half a day, but they were allowed six days and sixteen registration places in my constituency. Contrast this with the one day afforded by the political partisans who now control the lists in Manitoba.
In Gladstone under the management of the judges there were fifteen registration places which were kept open for one full week from 9 a.m. till 10 p.m., daily. Only one day was appointed for the sitting of the court of revision, but there was no limit on the duration of the sittings by the order in council. It is true the judges did not confine themselves to any particular hour or hours, the time for registration was' not limited by them and they could sit from day to day notwithstanding the fact that the attorney general took the position that they had no right to adjourn the court from day to day. The matter later came up in Winnipeg before the late Judge Kiliam, who decided that the judges had the right to adjourn their courts from time to time until they had finished their work. But the attorney general of the province took the position that they had not and disfranchised a number of people on that account, tearing from the votters' lists a certain number of electors who had registered that year.
I wish to make a comparison between the time allowed under the present law and under the previous law. Whereas in Gladstone in 1893, under the old arrangement we had sixteen registration places and six days for registration in 1893. in 1905. under political manipulation, we had only one day, one place and one registration clerk-and that clerk was only occupied in connection with the registration of voters for the whole territory from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., from
2.30	p.m. to 6 p.m., and from 7.30 p.m. to
9.30	p.m. Then the court of revision that was held following that registration allowed only five hours, from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., for revision. For the registration and the revision, the entire time allowed in connection with the compilation of the lists in that year was only twenty-two days. Under the law put in force by the Greenwav gov-

eminent, which has been referred to in this House as an iniquitous lawT, it was provided that not less than seventy days should be allowed in connection with the registration and revision of the lists. Contrast that with the present system by which only twenty-two days are allowed. This year there was even a shorter time than that. In the division from which I come, the whole time allowed for registration and revision is sixteen days. The law now in force in Manitoba is entirely under the control of the executive council of that province, the judges have nothing to say in connection with the preparation of the lists, they have nothing to do except to take evidence as to whether or not a man is entitled to be on the list. This is entirely different from the idea of the election law which hon. gentlemen opposite seek to convey.
I might put this concisely in the form of question and answer. Who limits the time for registration? The executive council of Manitoba. Who decides that there should be, but one registration clerk and one booth in each constituency? The executive council of Manitoba. Who fixes the places for registration booths and the hours during which they are to be open ? The executive council of Manitoba, the political machine. Who appoints the registration clerks who have very considerable discretionary powers The executive council of Manitoba. Who fixes the courts of revision allowing but for a single day or a part of a day or a number of days? Who fixes the time for the sittings of the court of revision and the duration of those sittings, who limits the hours during which the courts of revision can sit? The government of the province of Manitoba have full control over the courts of revision and everything else, in so far as registration and the revision of the voters' lists in the province of Manitoba are concerned. In fact the executive council of that province, the political machine, practically does everything in this matter and I do not hesitate to say that they manipulate and direct things to their own advantage. I have no hesitation in saying that because of the agitation that has been raised, because of the statements that are made in the press, because of the threatened hold-up of this government in this House the whole thing is done for one purpose and one only; they wish to continue every possible manipulation in connection with the preparation of the voters' lists in Manitoba. The government of Manitoba is not prepared to give to the people of that province the protection they are entitled to. We have not been getting that protection, and we are not getting it now. If they had wished to live up to the pledges they made before coming into power, they would have left on the statute-book the law of 1903 when the clean voters' list was prepared. In this connec-

tion, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) was pleased to refer last night to the Hon. Charles Mickle and to a statement attributed to that gentleman that these were clean voters' lists. I wired to Mr. Mickle asking him what he had to say about the election law and the administering of the same, and this is his answer :
The Act better in 1903. Neiv amendments have largely destroyed best features. Grievous complaints of unfair administration by government in many parts.
(Sgd.) C. J. MICKLE.
This is an entirely different showing of Hon. Mr. Mickle's opinion from that given by the lion member for Marquette, last night. That hon. gentleman tried to lead the House and the country to believe that Mr. Mickle had a high opinion of the present law and its administration. The very contrary is the fact. What Mr. Mickle was talking about, when he said the list was a clean list and the best list ever prepared in Manitoba, was the list proposed in 1903 when everything was under the control and management of the judges and entirely free from party manipulation.
Mr. Mickle has been in the legislature since 1903. Has he ever made any complaint in that House of the present law ?

I have given Mr. Mickle's reply, and I think that is sufficient for the present. For the last few years we have had an agitation over the franchise and the compiling of the voters' lists in the province of Manitoba because the law and the administration of the law have not been what it ought to be. If there is one thing more than another that we should sacredly guard it is the citizens' right to vote. I am sure that my hon. friends opposite are honest enough to admit, in their quiet moments that it is up to us all to stand strongly against any manipulation of the people's franchise. But, owing to the fact that party lines are strictly drawn, party prejudices strong and the desire for party advantage great, many are prepared to do what they themselves cannot justify. We should take a broader view and try to make a law that will be just and fair to all.
Does this Bill do that ?

We have not in Manitoba to-day the conditions which, as I have Just said, we ought to have, but we expect, if this Bill is passed, to have the privilege of creating these conditions. We have heard a great deal about the large number of people disfranchised in Manitoba in the last Dominion election. We had an exhibition here last night by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W.' J. Roche)
that that hon. gentleman should be ashamed of-or, if not ashamed of his statements of last night, he should be ashamed of his position on the third of August, 1906. On that day, the hon. gentleman attended a banquet in his own district at which Hon. Robert Rogers made the statement that the Liberals had disfranchised 1,395 of the honest electors of Portage la Prairie. The hon. gentleman (Mr. W. J. Roche) sat there and allowed these statements to go unchallenged, to be published broadcast in the press, and last night we had his own statement that, so far as he knew everything was done right in Portage la Prairie. And it was. I defy him or any other man to show that even one man was disfranchised in Portage la Prairie.
Did Leach manipulate your lists as he did those of Provencher ?

I am not saying anything about Leach ; I am talking about yourself. I cannot understand an hon. member of this House who takes the position now taken by the hon. gentleman for Marquette, sitting at a banquet in his own division and allowing such statements as I have quoted to go uncontradicted.
No, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Greenway) referred to statements made by the Montreal ' Gazette,' and there are one or two statements that I wish to quote from that newspaper myself. I must say I am disappointed in the ' Gazette.' I had looked upon it as being the most honest Conservative newspaper in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is not saying very much.

Well, be that as it may, I can only say I am surprised that any newspaper of such standing would allow itself to be led into making statements that are not supported by any credible evidence. I have always felt that I could believe most of the statements in the columns of the Montreal ' Gazette,' but I find reiterated in those columns the same kind of statements as are published in far less reputable journals. I think the time has arrived when the minds of the people of Canada should be disabused of opinions which some people have sought to cultivate in them concerning the thin red line. I am satisfied that the people of this country have no idea of what the thin red line really meant. They do not know that instead of 9,399 of the honest electors of Manitoba being disfranchised, as stated by Hon. Robert Rogers, and repeated again and again in this country, there were not even 99-to say nothing about the odd 9,300. I cannot understand hon. gentlemen, members of any party, allowing their co-workers in that party to continue reiterating such

statements, knowing all the time that they are false in every particular. The Montreal * Gazette ' repeats what many others repeated, and as it refers to my own division, I certainly think that the representative of the Montreal 'Gazette' here today should ask that paper to take back statements made in their editorial of a short time ago on that subject. I think it is only justice to themselves and justice to the people that they should do so. I find the ' Mail and Empire ' practically in the same position, and X think they should do likewise. They pretend to be fair and honest, and to give honest expressions of opinion, they pretend to do it.
But they don't

Well, if they don't, then I take it all back, and there is no use suggesting to them to act fairly. However,
I hope there are some Tories in this country that are fair and reasonable people, but possibly we don't meet them, particularly amongst those who are engaged in active politics. Now to disabuse the minds of the people of a false impression, it might be well to repeat some facts in connection with the election of 1904, and I hope those papers that I have a little respect for will publish the figures that I am going to quote. The Hon. Robert Rogers, who is the mouthpiece of the Tory party in the province of Manitoba, said that the provincial constituency of Hamiota, in the Dominion constituency of my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) said there were 777 Conservatives disfranchised by the red line. Now how does this figure out? In 1903 the judges controlled the lists, an election was run on that list, and 740 votes were polled for the Conservative party in that election. In 1907 the total vote polled for the Conservative candidate was 737, and he won. But the Hon. Robert Rogers makes a statement that in 1904 there were 777 Conservatives disfranchised by the red line in Hamiota, and the highest number they can count for themselves, either in the election of 1903 or in that of 1907, was 740. So we must have found by the red line a few' more votes than they did. I think these figures should disabuse the minds of those who are inclined to be fair, of the impression sought to be conveyed by the Hon. Robert Rogers, the Minister of Public Works in the province of Manitoba. I think such exaggerated statements as he makes here should discredit him in the minds of the people of the whole country. Now take the provincial electoral division of Minnedosa, which is also in the constituency of Marquette. In the provincial election of 1903 the total Tory vote polled was 504; in the Dominion election there w7as polled for my hon. friend 521 votes, in the same territory. In the provincial election of 1907 there were polled 502. Still the Hori. Robert Rogers says Mr. CRAWFORD.
that in 1904 we disfranchised 200 Conservative votes. But even with these 200 disfranchised, there were 521 polled, or 17 more than were ever polled before. I think this proves conclusively that the statements of the Hon. Robert Rogers are not in keeping w'ith the facts. Now take the town of Hamiota. In 1903 there were 317 Conservative votes cast, and in 1904 there were 314 cast, only 3 less than in 1903. Now in 1907, you would think that on account of the Tory candidate having w'on, and on account of the increase in population, there would be many more votes polled, and we find the Conservative candidate winning in 1907. Everything was then under the control of the powers that be in Manitoba, and the hon. gentleman who so severely criticised the red line, only polled 317 votes, just 3 more than were polled by the Conservatives in 1904. Still the Hon. Robert Rogers makes the statement that in the towTn of Hamiota there were 147 Conservatives disfranchised. Now take the Crandall poll. In 1903, 199 votes were polled; in 1904, 203, 4 more Conservative votes polled at the Crandall poll when this red line was used, than there were in the previous year when no red line was used. Still the Hon. Robert Rogers makes the statement that there were 172 Conservative voters disfranchised at that time Take the district of Marquette. In 1903 there w'ere 4,526 Conservative votes polled, and iu the next year there were polled for the hon. member for Marquette 5,115, or 489 more Tory votes polled in 1904 than in 1903; notwithstanding the statement of the Hon. Robert Rogers that in that territory there were, 1,919 Conservative voters disfranchised. F think these figures prove conclusively that the statements of the Hon. Robert Rogers, Minister of Public Works for the province of Manitoba, cannot be relied upon in any shape or form. I think the people of Canada who have been more or less disturbed in connection with this red line, feeling that wrong has been done, will hereafter discredit the statements of the Hon. Robert Rogers and w'ill come to the conclusion that the Liberals are at least as honset, and perhaps a little more so, than our Conservative friends.
Now w'hat do we find further? I have here a document prepared by our Conservative friends opposite in which they make use of the same startling statements. In this document they talk about the red line as one of the scandals that will be referred to in the coming Dominion elections. The heading is
Between 9,000 and 10,000. Additional light is thrown upon this steal bv the statement of the Hon. Robert Rogers, Minister of Public Works, who has made an examination of the red line list, and declared that 9,399 electors were disfranchised by this process
He declares that 9,399 electors were disfranchised by this process. Well, the follow-

ing is the record by constituencies. Marquette, 1,919, I think I have proved by the votes east in Marquette at that time that statement is entirely false and untrue. Proven-cher, 568 ; Portage la Prairie, 1,395. There is positive evidence, admitted by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche), that there was no truth in any shape, so far as Portage la Prairie is concerned, in that statement; and that being the case, every statement with regard to the red line by the politicians of Manitoba, backed up by Messrs. Roblin, Rogers and Campbell, fall to the ground entirely.
Will the hon. gentleman read that article all through? We would like to hear it all.

I think it would not be any harm. I will read a portion anyway. It is just a sample of the campaign stuff which our Conservative friends are distributing throughout the country, and I would like to warn the people of Canada of the nature of the statements being put out at this time to discredit the Liberals of this country-statements entirely false and untrue.
Would the hon. gentleman kindly read that portion of my speech, as contained in ' Hansard,' in which I sad that in Portage la Prairie there was no fraud in connection with the lists ?
If the hon. gentleman likes he may read it himself.
J ROCHE I did not say that at all and I challenge the hon. gentleman to point that out in my speech.

In connection with this red line business and the possibility of the people continuing under the present situation, I may say that we have to get away from anything which will keep us in that condition of strife and discussion and of unfair dealings in connection with the preparation of the lists.
Show where it is unfair.
Where what is unfair ?
The way we make up our voters' lists.
I have shown that, under the present administration in Manitoba things are manipulated purely for political advantage, and that Is what we want to get away from.
You make that assertion.
Yes.
But you have not proved it.

I have proved it to the satisfaction of myself and I think of many more in this country. To show that even at present we cannot afford to go on in the present situation, I have the voters' lists prepared last year and revised, and what is the situation with regard to one poll? Poll No. 13 in the local constituency of South Brandon, part of which is in the constituency of Brandon and part in the federal division of Brandon-in that poll there is .a list of electors, and we have in the 1904 election 63 votes in the lists supplied the returning officer on the Brandon side and 3 on the Portage la Prairie side. In the lists prepared in 1907, we find in that poll 5S names only, one of which belonged to the division of Portage la Prairie and 57 to the division of Brandon.
The next matter I shall deal with in connection with the red line will be with regard to the committee which was appointed by this House and the statements made before that committee by Mr. Knott, who acted on behalf of the province of Manitoba in connection with the prosecutions. Mr. Knott gave evidence before that committee, and you will find, on examining his evidence, that the conclusions he came to were these. Mr. Knott stated positively that, in so far as the adjusting of constituencies and the polling divisions in the province of Manitoba by the returning officers was concerned, they did the only thing they could do. It was the only reasonable way of doing it. That is Mr. Knott's statement under oath before the committee at that time. You will find on page 51 of the evidence that he was asked the question :
Can you tell me any way how he can get a list except in the way in which it has been suggested, as you say, he did here by a red line throughout, as the Manitoba Act says he should do with names that are to be struck off.
I might repeat what was said the other day by the Minister of Justice, namely, that the Manitoba Act provides that when names are being erased or struck off in any way, the means used shall be either a red or a black line. In this case the returning officer used a red line.
Q. He did here by a red line throughout, as the Manitoba Act says he should do, with names that are to be struck off ?-A. IJnder what circumstances?
Q. In the case of overlapping?-A. I have stated my opinion very fairly, I think, what in that case his duty should be.
Q. His duty would be to do what lie did here?-A. There is no doubt about that; of course he might do something else, bnt I think that would be a reasonable thing to do.
That is Mr. Knott's statement before the committee in connection with this red line situation. And, as I have said before, Mr. Knott was the prosecuting attorney in those cases in Manitoba and appeared before the



committee on behalf of the red line situation and the local government, and he made the positive statement that the right thing to do was to do just what was done, and that was draw a red line through the names. Further on Mr. Knott repeats this. The question was asked:
How is ihe to get, except in the way he did-
I am simply speaking about the matter of striking out the names, of using the red lines -how else was he to get a proper list for the polling division of the federal constituency out of the local registration lists. Can you tell me how else he can do that?-A. I said at first, I think the reasonable thing would be to do what was done. I think I stated that two or three times before.
Those are the words of Mr. Knott.
He goes on to say, referring to the overlapping. that if he had the legal right to do it there was no other way of doing it than the way he did it.
Did he say he had the legal right?
Yes, in connection with the overlapping.
Did he say that Mr. Leach had the legal right to draw the red line?
You had better read it all :

All right:
The Dominion returning officers, the attorney general claims, were not, however, justified in subdividing provincial polling divisions which were entirely within the limits of Dominion constituencies. It is to be borne in mind that at the provincial elections in 1903, there were subdivisions of polling divisions in undoubted contravention of the law, in no less than 17 of the local constituencies. It is an open secret that these subdivisions were made, not by the returning officers but by officials of the government in the legislative buildings on Kennedy street working under the direction of the government.
Then Mr. Hooper says :
Evidently your assertion is made on the same authority as similar statements were given to a committee of the House of Commons in 1906, &c.
Your editorial, if allowed to pass unanswered, would emphasize the impression then attempted to be left on the public mind that the civil .servants of Manitoba are lacking in spirit of honesty and integrity-therefore, I hope you will give space to the following letters received from the returning officers in the provincial elections of 1903.
Now, this is what I want to call particular attention to. This is Mr. Hooper's statement in regard to different returning officers in different electorai districts in the province of Manitoba dividing the polling divisions :
As far as I know these are bhe only returning officers who created new polling divisions that year.
Then he gives the names of these officers as follows : H. Archibald, Melita ; W. G. Hetherington, Souris: S. T. Parr, Neepawa ;

If the vote of that man can be traced back it will be known whether he was properly qualified to vote or not, and that is a reasonable and proper precaution to ensure fair-play at the election. Now, Mr. Speaker, I approve of this legislation along the lines of the present Bill and I will do all I can to see that it is passed. No matter how our friends opposite may threaten it will make no difference in my stand, and I am afraid that the style of operating which they have adopted will only tend to [DOT]keep us further apart and to prevent us getting together and deciding on what should be the proper form of this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I have followed with a great deal of Interest the discussion which has taken place upon the second reading of this Bill. Indeed, I think that no subject-matter which has come before the House during the present session has been as interesting as the one now under discussion. For my own part, I say frankly and sincerely that the Bill seemed harmless when I first read it; but after having listened to this discussion, I look upon it as one of the most pernicious, most mischievous and most wicked pieces of legislation that has come under my notice since I have had the honour of a seat in this House. It is so qualified by me unreservedly because its object is to depart in a clandestine manner from the principle which this House adopted in 1898, so far as may be necessary to control the results of the election which is about to take place. This is something new to me at any rate. We have had election frauds of a very grave and serious character-far more serious within the last few years than formerly. Under the old forms of influence the elector at least had knowledge of the manner in which his vote was disposed of through direct means of corruption. But we have had another stage which consisted in influencing an election by spoiling, stealing and switching ballots. I say this because there has been abundant proof of it, irrespective entirely of what side has been guilty. There has been that form of undue influence over the free expression of the will of the people; and we have here a third form, which is perhaps more serious than any of the others, inasmuch as it cannot be guarded against. Without any regard to the will of those who are really the electors of a constituency, it will permit a government which is waning, which is moribund, which is failing, to influence the free expression of the will of a constituency. That is the way in which I understand this legislation, and I am quite open to conviction if my judgment in that regard is too severe. But taking that view of it, the House will understand that I look on it as an extremely serious measure which deserves our careful attention.
We in this country are continually comparing our institutions to those of England, saying that we live under the same regime and that the principles that obtain in England obtain here. That statement is only partially true. If you compare the manner in which subjects of this kind are treated in the mother of parliaments with the manner in which they are treated here, you will find that there are profound differences, which are to our dishonour and disfavour to such an extent that travellers from the old country who visit Canada constantly remark upon them to our detriment. Take the subject of the preparation of the electoral lists. We all know that in England that subject is always amicably discussed

and arranged between tbe parties before tbe law relating to it is enacted. The parties confer and something which is fair, reasonable and just is determined upon, and that becomes the matter of legislation. You will not find in England, during the past century or very nearly so, such a discussion as the one we are having here to-day. The distribution of seats is another matter which is arranged amicably between the parties, the discussion between them leading to something which incorporates British fair-play, and that becomes a matter of statute. Let me go a little further in order to speak of a matter which is uppermost in my mind, and which has been so for several weeks past. Take the question of the audit of the public accounts. Could there be anything more absolutely different in the two countries? Could there be anything more grotesque, more absurd, more unjust, than our way of proceeding with that audit, as compared with what obtains in England?

Hear, hear.
Mi-. MONK. 1 hear somebody say ' hear, hear,' on the other side of the House, and that is just the hon. gentleman who has contributed perhaps more than anybody else to accentuate those differences which are altogether to our discredit.
My hon. friend did not contribute very much one way or the other.

Well, my hon. friend has evoked from me an admission which is this. When I have been at the Public Accounts Committee, and have seen there my colleagues, to whom I cannot give too much praise, busying themselves with what in England is uncontradicted, untrammelled, unobstructed, and have seen the hon. gentleman and some of his colleagues doing what they were doing, courage has failed me, and I have preferred to give up the job. We all know that in England the public accounts are audited by a small committee of ten or twelve members, to which some others may perhaps be added.
It would be interesting to ascertain from our hon. friend how often he has attended the Public Accounts Committee before he gives any instructions with regard to it.

Let me ask my hon. friend what business he had there at all, because a man who has no subject-matter to be investigated in the Public Accounts Committee in England never thinks of setting his foot there to obstruct those who have. I am speaking of constitutional usage and I say, without fear of contradiction that a member of parliament in England who would go to a committee having any such matter as this before it, in order to object to the questions of others would arouse such public indignation that within 24 hours he would be compelled to resign.
Has my hon. friend tendered his resignation? Because I have seen him often asking questions in matters in which he had no special interest or which he did not bring before the committee himself.

I may have done so in trying to help the investigator, but I think that any sensible man will admit that is a very different thing from sitting there as a counsel, as a lawyer, fed, engaged, paid, one would say-I do not say that was the case, but I say bore the appearance of a court and we were there in the presence of people who were obstructing the investigation.
I do not wish to prolong discussion with my hon. friend upon that subject, but I say it is another example of the difference which we find between British parliamentary institutions and our i interpretation of them here. There the chairman of such a committee is always a member of the opposition, the investigation we know covers the administration, so to speak, of the British empire, compared with which our own investigation must necessarily appear extremely small and puny. Where do you find the difficulty in England ? These 10 or 15 men go through the accounts, every opportunity is given for the fullest investigation, there is no question of proof or the nature of evidence, there are no men there occupying the singular and contradictory position of, being members themselves, having found nothing whatever to investigate and being there for the sole purpose of blocking the investigations of others. Could one imagine anything more abusive than our usage in this respect of what we call the British constitution and British practice? But let us go a step further. When in England, Sir, as happens at least every ten years-and I think it should happen every ten years here, because I am a great admirer of the political institutions of the mother country-a government feels itself falling, as the present imperial government feels itself falling to a certain extent even at this moment, the cabinet, in a quiet and dignified manner, accepts the situation and awaits patiently and calmly the verdict of the people. But in Canada, almost invariably-and here is a flagrant instance of it-there'is an endeavour made, by some crooked wicked mischievous legislation, to prevent the result, to thwart the will of the people, to prevent that free expression of popular will by some hook or crook, as we will see it is intended by this section, and thus to delay the fatal hour. That is the conclusion at which I have arrived in respect of the purpose of this legislation. But I have not by any means lost confidence in my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). He did not prepare this legislation, it is not he who drafted this Act. I have noticed with what care he has attended to and taken notes of the dis-

cussion which has taken place. I do not think the Minister of Justice himself, personally, of his own hand, has drafted that disposition. It comes from that part of the country which it is especially designed to affect and although it may have gone through the hands of the Minister of Justice, I say that he was not the inspirer of it; I know the hon. gentleman and that is my belief. I have confidence in my right hon. friend, I have known him for a long time. We were trained under the same legal master.

Now let me as briefly as possible point out what obtains in our province as regards the electoral lists. I am quoting from the Quebec Elections Act of 1885, and pointing out how our lists are prepared. From the 1st to the 15th of every month of September, under article 19 of that Act, the secretary treasurer prepares his electoral lists, and gives notice of its publication. If the secretary treasurer fails to prepare the electoral lists within that delay he may be ordered to do so by a judge, or a judge may order another person to do so in his place. After the lists is prepared there are 15 days given for complaints to be made. The secretary treasurer has made his list, he has posted it up and given public notice, and 15 days are given for complaints in writing. Then the complaints are taken up with the electoral lists at a special meeting of the council. The council hears these complaints, revises the list and finally decrees that the list is in force. Then you still have thirty days in which to appeal from the decision of council to a judge of the Superior Court. That is briefly the routine followed in our province. Since I have been in this House I have heard a great deal about electoral lists, the manner of making them, and the procedure, and I doubt if there is a simpler or better way of preparing lists than that. Nobody knows better than a municipal councillor the qualifications of a man to be an elector. As a rule, the councillors are not of the same political colour. Their decisions are sometimes unfair, and appeals are taken; but there is always the appeal from a judge to a judge, and that appeal is generally satisfactory. If there is no organized municipality in any territory, it would be undoubtedly the duty of the secretary treasurer of the county council, which has jurisdiction in that case, to prepare a list and to go through exactly the same formality. He would have to post it up, it would come up for review before the county council this time, not before the local council, and there would be an appeal to a judge. I think that confirms what my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) stated, that the province of Quebec was brought in here as a pretext, because there is no need of this provision in Quebec.

The secretary treasurer of each municipality shall between the first and fifteenth day'of the month of March, in each year, make in duplicate subdivided for each polling subdivision, a list in alphabetical order, of all persons, who according to the valuation roil then dn force in the municipality for municipal purposes, appear to be electors by reason of the real estate possessed or occupied by them in any manner within the municipality, or by reason of being otherwise qualified as set forth in article 9.
The valuation roll is the principal guide which is used in the local municipalities, but in the case mentioned by my right hon. friend, the latter part of that article applies * or by reason of being otherwise qualified as set forth in article 9.' It has been decided by our courts that the valuation roll is to a certain extent the guide as to the qualification of the voter, but it is not the only one. A man may be put on the electoral lists who is not on the valuation roil at all. For instance, a man who earns $300 a year in our province is not on the valuation roll, yet he has the right to be on the voters' list, because in our province any man who earns $300 a year, is a British subject, and of the proper age, has the right to be on the voters' list. Now, there is no doubt whatever that -we have no unorganized municipal territory within our province. My hon. friend from Bellechasse would perhaps be surprised if I told him that, although I have written to a number of people asking for information in regard to this Bill, people residing very far from each other within the limits of my province, and people conversant with the electoral law, they all answer in exactly the same way, and I will place these letters at any time at the disposal of my right hon. friend. The object of this Bill is unfairly to obtain the right of franchise for men engaged on government works; that is the answer which I received from every one of these people.
The object is to use that part of the Act in order to have special officers named and have them make special electoral lists which will enable people, working within the limits of a province, upon the Transcontinental or other public work, to obtain the franchise for the purposes of the next general election. There is no doubt that

is the object, and I consider that the opposition are right in refusing to allow the passage of such a measure. My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) is quite justified in saying that the province of Quebec Is brought into this enactment under a false pretense. There is no unorganized territory there.
Does my hon. friend know as a matter of fact that the county treasurer does prepare the lists for those unorganized territories even if they are within his county ?
I do not. My hon. friend will understand that there are very few people residing out of the purview of a local municipality.
If he does not do it, does my hon. friend argue that these people are not entitled to their franchise?

They are undoubtedly, but there are very few, if any, who exist. If there are any, they have their recourse. The treasurer should perform his duty as regards those electors. If he does not, the machinery is there and can be brought into requisition in five minutes. The secretary-treasurer may be required to make an elec-, toral list for those voters. That list will' be subject to revision before a county council and there may be an appeal to a judge, but that is a very different thing from coming in on the eve of an election with a returning officer, who may not be very scrupulous-and while there are very honest returning officers there may be some who are not

and going through those outside localities and placing 300 or 400 men on the list, without giving any chance of revision, without notice, without any recourse of appeal to the county council or the judge. That is the opinion entertained in tlie province of Quebec by everybody, Liberal as well as Conservative, who takes the trouble of looking over that enactment and has any knowledge of the working of our electoral law.

It occurs to me that this amendment is not in order. Under the British North America Act it is provided that:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or Bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue or of any tax or impost to any purpose that is not recommended to that House by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address or Bill is passed.
I take it that the real meaning and construction of these words is that no charge shall be imposed on the public revenue without a Bill or resolution for the purpose being first recommended by His Excellency the Governor General. By this Bill it is declared, in the first place, that the Governor General in Council shall have the power to take over all the branch lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I think there can be no question that if the resolution stopped there it would be clearly out of order, because that would enable the Governor in Council to take over these roads, no matter what they might cost, and, of course, appropriate the moneys of the country for that purpose. It is very clear that*a Bill of that kind could not be proposed to parliament except upon the recommendation of the Governor General in Council. Then it is also provided by the first part of the resolution that the government shall have power to proceed to a valuation of the company's property, take all necessary steps for that purpose, and, therefore necessarily incur any expense which might be necessary for the purpose of having an arbitration. That clearly would be also a charge upon the revenue. The amount, therefore, which, if this amendment passed the country would have to pay for these branch lines, would be fixed and determined by arbitration in the manner which this amendment suggests. There you have by the first part of the amendment authority given to the Governor General in Council to take over all these branches and also provision to take the necessary steps for arbitration and necessarily incident to that power, to incur whatever expenses would be necessary in order to take those proceedings. You have also a provision as to the mode in which the valuation shall be arrived at, that is to say from the valuation shall be deducted any subsidies which may have been paid. The only question to my mind is whether the proviso at the close nrevents the prin-

Therefore, this seems to me to be an amendment which would be clearly within the prohibition of section 54 of the British North America Act, and which could only be brought before parliament by a message from His Excellency the Governor General.
