If my hon. friend looks at the supplementary agreement of the National Transcontinental Railway, 1904, he will probably not find that any sanction was obtained from His Excellency the Governor General on that occasion. The principle is the same, we get the option to take over the works, but whether we shall exercise that option or not is for us to determine when the 50 year period has expired. We are not committing ourselves by securing this option in the interest of the people to the extent of one cent. I am not asking the appropriation of one cent in this matter. I am asking parliament and the government, who should be the guardians of the people, to avail themselves of the opportunity they now have of securing the necessary condition to the granting of this extension of time, a condition which costs this parliament and the people of Canada not one cent, which appropriates not one cent out of the revenues, but which secures for the people something they ought to have, the possibility of not only obtaining these branch lines but of obtaining them on something like reasonable terms when the time arrives. I would like to ask the members of the government: when that provision was inserted in the Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Bill, a provision similar to the one we have here-not worded in the same way, but providing that parliament may ^alce over that work-did we get the sanction of His Excellency the Governor General on that occasion ? No : we did not think of such a thing. And that emanated from the government themselves, it was a provision introduced by the Minister of Railways and Canals, as I assume. It is perfectly idle, I submit, to raise this objection. I am surprised that my distinguished and learned friend the Minister of Public Works, astute lawyer and able counsel as he is, should suggest for a moment that this is a question of the appropriation of money. You have only to read the statute on one hand and the provision of this amendment on the other to see instantly that this is not a question of appropriating money. But, granted that he is right in saying that before we can complete this option we should obtain the sanction of His Excellency the Governor General, still, as a first step, it would be submittetd to parliament, and it would be so submittted only after His Excellency had given his approval for the taking over of the lines. I submit that this is only an option at the most; there is no pretense of appropriating one dollar of the revenues of Canada by reason of the condition which, I submit, should be annexed to the granting of this extension of time to this railway company.

If no other gentleman wishes to speak, I desire to say just a

word. Before dealing with the question itself, I may perhaps not improperly remark that I think it is a pity that my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox), called upon as he was simply to discuss a constitutional question, should have thought it worth while to go far out of his way to suggest that there was some impropriety in the fact of my taking this objection. I exercised my right as a member of the committee to raise what seemed to me a good and substantial point of order.
Now, with regard to the original agreement between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific, the hon. gentleman suggests that he doubts whether that agreement was submitted to parliament with the approval of His Excellency. I cannot imagine that he is correct in that. I take it for granted that the agreement had received the consent of His Excellency and was so submitted to parliament. I have no doubt whatever that that was the case and I think anybody would say that it was necessary before parliament could properly consider it.
Now, I do not know that the case of the Shuswap Boom Company could be any precedent for action by you on this occasion because the provision in that Bill was altogether different from the provision here. This Bill proposes that the government shall take certain steps before coming to parliament, that it shall proceed to value all these properties, that it shall incur the obligation of having an arbitration and with power to appeal, and that all that shall be done
Not necessarily.

Yes, before coming to parliament. And then, if the consent of parliament was given, it would go through. But all these things have to be done before coming to parliament; and I submit that this imposes a money obligation on the country which can only be imposed by parliament upon tluj initiation of the government and the consent of the Governor General.
I wish only to say a few' words
X am sorry-if I had known the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) was going to speak, I would not have closed-
We are in committee and can speak as often as we like.

In 1904, parliament, in its wisdom, thought of protecting the future interests of the people of Canada by reserving certain rights in branch lines which might be built by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. After full consideration, that protection was passed by this parliament under the guidance of the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid
Laurier) and his ministers. We have now a palpable attempt to evade the protection that was then given to the people of this country and to enable the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to get rid of the right then reserved to the people by putting up a mere fiction company belonging to themselves-virtually the same company -which will build the branches and set the people of Canada at defiance. And this is being done with the knowledge of the right hon. gentleman and his cabinet. There is no concealing the fact; the truth is apparent on the face of it.
I rise to a point of order. It seems to me that it is very irregular for an hon. gentleman, in discussing a point of order, to travel outside and to attribute motives.
We are discussing the amendment.
No, a point of order has been raised.
Unless the clause is passed, I will discuss the point itself.

The point of order has not been ruled upon.
Mr. FOSTER I can hardly yet think that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) can be serious in raising this as a point of order
He is, very serious.

It certainly was surprising to me to hear the hon. gentleman. I have had quite a long experience in this House, and it surprises me to hear it argued that we cannot give advice and embody that advice, in a resolution or even in an Act, with reference to precautions that should be taken to safeguard the public interest. This is what is authorized:
' The Governor shall thereupon and thereafter have the right to take over

.'
That is all that this amendment proposes to ask. Then, at the last, we have the words:
Provided that nothing in this Act contained shall authorize the government to take over the.said lines of railway or any of them without the consent of parliament, previously obtained.
Consent obtained for what? To the exercise of such rights. But before doing that we should get the authority of parliament to exercise that right. So I take it they will have no authority at all, even on that point. You go to work and make valuations, spend money, do anything at all until you have asked parliament and until parliament has exercised that right.
Then what is the object?

The object is to preserve the right of the people to do that if they

please, and so to preserve the public interest.
Parliament can do that at any time.

But parliament, sitting now and giving this extension to this peculiar company, thinks it is better, and haviag a perfect right to think so, to put that proviso in and so safeguard what they consider to be in the public interest.

I think it is my duty to endeavour to get the leader of the government to take some definite attitude with reference to this matter. I would like to see the government realize what their duty is, and I would like to see the right hon. gentleman realize his duty, because he is more than anybody else responsible for what we should now do. He is an old parliamentarian; he realizes the gravity of a proposition of this kind. Because a private member of this House! wants to submit something that he believes is in the public interest, something which will never cost the country a dollar unless parliament sees fit to exercise the rights and privileges there secured, to say that a private" member in the discharge of his duty cannot bring in a constitutional amendment to safeguard the rights of the people, because if that right is exercised by the government, it win cost money; to say that no private member has a right to submit an amendment which will give the country the right to acquire the property if parliament says so at the end of fifty years-I say that is a startling proposition. I appeal with confidence to the right hon. gentleman on account of his great experience. I always feel that I can with a good deal more confidence appeal to him than I can to some other members of the cabinet. I am sorry that the Minister of Public Works thinks I said something that was not complimentary.
I think you were not discussing the constitutional point.

I will admit that. But I doubt whether my hon. friend relied much on the objection he takes. Astute lawyer as he is, always actuated by honest motives as lawyers are, I feel that he put it forward for what it was worth, and realized at the time that it wasn't worth very much. Now, in order to impress this matter upon the leader of the government, I wish to refer to the Act from which I take this clause.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Let us dispose of the point of order. I intend to refer the matter to the Speaker in consequence of its importance. If there was no proviso I would declare the point of order well taken.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have had the opportunity of listening to the discussion and Mr. FOSTER.
am inclined to rule that the point is not well taken. The amendment proceeds in the first place to state :
In case the government, as defined in the schedule to the National Transcontinental Railway Act, 1903, in pursuance of the terms of the said schedule, shall at any time determine to underbake the operation of the eastern division of the National Transcontinental Railway, the government shall thereupon and thereafter have the right to take over

And so on. The amendment down to the word 1 provided ' is unquestionably within the rule, and the point would be well taken. But the words following the word ' provided ' :
That nothing in this Act contained shall authorize the government to take over the said lines of railway or any of them without the consent of parliament, previously obtained.
Modify the earlier portion and would preclude, as I view it, the possibility of the expenditure of any money for the purpose without the consent of parliament being first obtained, and then would be the time to procure the consent of the Governor General and submit the matter by resolution to the House.

I regret that I was interrupted in the few remarks I was about to make by the astute Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). Having heard so much about his astuteness, I would beat-most inclined to think he had directed that astuteness to-night to raising a point of order in order that it might prevent the completion of the discussion before nine o'clock. I suppose that- the Bill, under the order of the House, will now have to stand over; but being so very astute, it may be difficult to know in what particular direction he was displaying that astuteness. I was saying that in the Act of 1904, this government, at the instance of hon. members on this side, had made provision to protect the interests of the people in years to come. When the provinces were so progressing that no man could at that time foresee what might be the general public interest in the future, we thought it absolutely essential, looking forward to that future to provide that, should the leased property be surrendered, we should have the right to take over branches that might be absolutely essential to the main property. In all fairness, honesty and statesmanlike prevision, we consider that we were entitled to provide proper protection. Therefore we did provide that, in certain eventuality, we should have the right to take over certain branches, if parliament saw fit. Now, what is being done, palpably done, to evade that provision and done-if the right hon. gentleman and his cabinet did not see it. they know it now-with the apparent and almost positive intention of evading the

condition parliament imposed in 1904? We have the right by act of parliament to take over certain branch lines, should it be in the interests of the country to take them over. The hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Knowles) asked how do we know that the people then interested in these branch lines companies will be the same as the Grand Trunk Pacific to-day? What a wonderfully shrewd motion that is. We know who are interested in that company to-day. We know that the effect of the Acts they are trying to get through this House will be to evade a condition imposed upon the Grand Trunk Pacific in the public interest. And if they bring in a Bill here, under their own auspices, a Bill in which, beyond all doubt or question, nobody else to-day is interested -if they bring in a Bill to enable them to take out of that contract what may be most valuable property, why should we not put on record in the Acts of parliament that the company they form are bound by the original contract, so that those who become associated with them may know the terms upon which they come in and will be bound as the Grand Trunk Pacific would be and as they ought to be.
Do I understand my hon. friend to say that the clause proposed is identical with the one in the original Act referring to the Grand Trunk Pacific itself? I think it is far different.
Will my hon. friend bring in the original clause?
That would not be an answer to my question.	*

It is a very common and ancient custom to answer one question by asking another. But are we to go on year after year and never get more enlightened? The hon. gentleman himself has had an opportunity of knowing what was thought right in 1904. But he is going backward. Are we not therefore to go forward? If we find a weakness, if there be a weakness in what was then proposed, why should we not correct it? Or shall we do as the Minister of Railways and Canals proposes, cut away our protection altogether? Surely there can be no question as to what we should do. What possible excuse has this company to come here and say that the branch lines which, in the original contract, were to be built by the company, subject to certain rights on the part of the people of Canada, shall, by our own acts and concurrence, be allowed to be built by somebody else who will not be bound by those conditions. Why, talk to any business man on such a subject and he will say that the proposition is one of pure idiocy. Does the hon. gentleman suppose that if, as an individual, he were making a bargain and were a shareholder or proprietor or interested in the contract, he would be taken in by such a palpable evasion. I give him
credit for too much common sense to believe it. But of course he is only dealing for the people of Canada, and we know what, the late Mr. Vanderbilt is supposed to have said about the public.

What did he say ?
Progress reported.

The hour for private Bills having expired, the House resumed consideration of the second reading of Bill (No. 115) to amend the Dominion Elections Act and the proposed amendment of Mr. W. J. Roche thereto.

As I said, Mr. Speaker, before you rose at six o'clock, what impressed me most, during this discussion regarding what took place in Manitoba, is the failure by hon. gentlemen opposite to deny that what is called ' the thin red line ' was perpetrated either by Leach himself or under his direction. Surely if any alterations had to be made in the electoral lists, they came naturally under the purview of the returning officer in each constituency. Although there may not be any provision especially in the Act, under the circumstances in which those alterations were made, the returning officer was called upon, in common fairness and justice, to notify the candidates before making any changes. Did he notify those with regard to whom he intended altering the lists? No, the alterations were made by a person or persons having an authority; and once made, whatever might have been their effect-whether they cancelled entirely the names of the voters or transferred them to distant polls is a matter of no importance although one as to which there has been a great deal of quibbling-those alterations should have been brought to the knowledge of those who were affected. But we have no excuse whatever offered in that regard. The whole discussion has impressed me with the absolute certainty that what was perpetrated that time was the result of a preconceived scheme which successfully worked the disastrous results that have been subsequently condemned on all sides.
My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie spoke at great length of defects in the present Manitoba law, but to my mind none of these defects were of a really grave character and none confuted the crowning principle that finally this making of the lists in Manitoba comes under the view of the judge, as it does in the province of Quebec. There are defects in the electoral law of the province of Quebec but that does not mean that our electoral law is not a singularly satisfactory one. Even admitting that defects do exist in Manitoba that is no ground for the sweeping change this Bill contemplates. When in 1898 we decided to adopt the provincial

lists iu principle did we not know that defects would be found in the provincial laws exactly as defects were found under our own Dominion Franchise Act ? It is the merest flimsy pretext to say that because in some particular respect the electoral law of a province is deficient we will sweep aside the principle we adopted in 1898 and on the eve of an election and after the issue of the writs, that the government will take unto itself the entire preparation of the voters' lists. The amendment of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) after laying down the truism that this Bill discriminates against Manitoba and British Columbia compared with the other provinces, declares:
That this law is a radical departure from the principle of accepting provincial voters' lists and is invidious and unjustifiable.
I stated this afternoon that there is no unorganized territory within the limits of the province of Quebec and that therefore there is no justification for this enactment in reference to Quebec, because the whole province is organized municipally and under the provincial law every man who has the right to vote can be placed upon the list by the proper officer. My right hon. friend may ask : if such be the same, why do I fear the passage of this enactment.
There is unorganized territory in Quebec.
Where?
In the county of Wright which I represent there are 572,397 acres of unorganized territory.

My hon. friend was not here this afternoon when I placed before the House what I think was an unanswerable argument. Let me repeat for his benefit that every piece of territory in the province of Quebec is under the control of a municipal council and it is therefore organized.

It comes under the municipal code in as much as it may be under the control of the county council, but it may not necessarily be organized into a municipality and the residents of a township which has no municipal organization would not have the right to vote unless they have property in an adjoining township.

My hon. friend is mistaken. Let him look at article 32 of the municipal code, which says: That if there is no local municipality in any given place within the limits of the county-and all parts of the province of Quebec are within the limits of a county-then the county council replaces the local municipality, and so the secretary is obliged to prepare a list of electors for these 500,000 acres my hon. friend refers to, exactly as would the secre-Mr. MONK.
tary treasurer of a local council. There can be no doubt whatever about that, and I will not discuss the point further. True, there is no local council and there are no local councillors, but, if there are not the very small number of people required by our municipal code to form a municipal council, in that case the administration is by the county council.
Does the county council make electoral lists?

Our electoral law prescribes that the secretary treasurer of the council, whatever council it may be, must make an electoral list, and if he has under his control territory which belongs properly to the county council where there is no local municipal organization, he should make an electoral list for that part of his territory. There is no question about that whatever. My hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Duncan Ross) asked me had I any knowledge of a case where a county secretary treasurer had made such a list and my reply to him is that I have not, and the reason is because there are not many places where there is no local council. But if there were such a place the duty of the officer would be perfectly plain, and if he did not fulfil his duty under the provisions of our election law any party interested could apply to a judge for a remedy, and the judge could order the secretary treasurer to prepare the electoral lists.
What control has this parliament over such an officer ?

We have no more control over him than over any other municipal officer, but parliament has adopted the principle that we shall take out lists from these municipal officers. We receive the electoral lists from the registrars who receive them from the secretary treasurer and the registrar is a municipal officer. It is true they grumble about it but nevertheless they forward copies of these lists to Ottawa and so far no difficulty has been experienced. In fact when this franchise question was discussed in this parliament in 1908, I spoke of it in my own county, and knowing that generally speaking our provincial lists are well made, I took the ground that I was not opposed to the change, and I think our experience in the province of Quebec has justified me in that. That being the case, and I know it is a fair subject for discussion, and it is because it is a fair subject for discussion that I have most fear. Here are already two hon. gentlemen from the province of Quebec who mention large areas in that province where there is no possibility of having an electoral list. That is what my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) has stated.
There will be every possibility under this Bill.

My hon. friend takes the ground at the present moment that there is no possibility. If that were the case, then I would have to admit that there is a large desolate area iu the province of Quebec where there are very few people, where it is very easy to send people, and where people might spring up suddenly like Cadmus' soldiers, and those people would have to be provided with the electoral franchise.
In the county of Wright they all vote honestly.

I have no doubt about that. There was an old French Canadian In my county who said that he believed everybody was perfectly honest, but that he had misgivings about everybody. What would happen in the province of Quebec would be that this enabling enactment would enable the government on the eve of an election, after the Issue of the writ, to send out persons to make electoral lists. I know of ten or twelve or fifteen constituencies in the province of Quebec which would be liable to this kind of invasion. How do I know that in my own constituency, almost an urban constituency, portions of which are densely populated, some gentlemen oil the eve of the election would not find some spot unorganzed municipality in his opinion. where he would have to make a list ? I say this is a most dangerous enactment so far as the province of Quebec .is concerned. The Transcontinental Railway is at present under construction through several of those constituencies-through parts where there is no municipal organization. If the idea propounded bv the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) and the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin), and sustained by the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Ross), be correct, there will be th? opportunity to send in an officer to prepare a list, conforming himself, says the Bill, as far as possible to the law. Well, there is only one law, and it is perfectly clear, that is, that you can only make an electoral list between the 1st and the loth of September. IIow can a man go in there and make a list at any time, and how can he, between the issue of the writ and the final event, conform even in the slightest degree to those dispositions of our Electoral Act, which require two stages-a revision by a council of men, jurymen, so to speak, with a right of final appeal to a judge thirty days after? And what will be the position of a candidate who does not happen to be a friend of the parties carrying out this scheme ? Will he run up into those far northern latitudes in order to find out whether lists are being prepared, and leave the rest of the constituency, where are the legally qualified electors ? The truth is that in 258
these cases he will have to trust to chance, and wait patiently until some time after the election, when these parties have returned to the proper seat of the election, and reported as to the results. That is the position, and I say that it places in doubt a considerable proportion of the electoral districts of the province of Quebec. What we are asked to do this evening is to sanction that principle, which is really a return, under a slightly varied form, to the old rotten borough system as it existed in England before the Reform Bill. It is nothing else. We know from past experience that these things are possible. The men who would be suddenly brought into constituencies would be the legitimate successors of what used to be called the pot-wallopers

people brought into a constituency at the last minute in order to change the free expression of the will of the people. Our hon. friends may argue that this is to sujipose that the government would abuse its powers. Governments do abuse their powers as much now as they did before the Reform Bill, and to ask us to allow that latitude is to expose us to the danger of the intolerable oppression that existed before the passage of that same Reform Bill. Under these circumstances what is our duty ? It seems to me that our duty is very clear-it is to resist the granting of such power, to resist the possibility of a renewal of those abuses. I speak only for myself. We have in our hands a remedy, which is the old remedy which enabled the people of England to secure the redress of the great grievances from which they suffered during centuries, that is, to refuse supply to the government until they have abandoned this unjust and unfair pretension ; and I tell you, Mr. Speaker, and this House, that as far as I am concerned, that being the only remedy in our hands, I will avail myself of it to the fullest extent. This is not the case of an ordinary grievance. It is not the case of applying under ordinary circumstances the old adage that redress goetn before supply. This is not a question of policy ; it is not a question of a grievance which at a later date can be cured ; it is not a question of a grievance as to which there can be any doubt ; it is a question of an imminent danger of opnression. That is the way I view it. We are more or less on the eve of an election, and the government ask this House for power to control the franchise in the constituencies, under circumstances which are but th'nly veiled in this enactment-the old abuse by which the Crown prevented the free expression of the will of the people during such a long time in England.
It is for us at the present moment, for those of us at least who do not feel disposed to grant that exorbitant power, to resist it by all the means at our command and the means to my mind are very plain. They are to refuse the grant of supplies. The



government asks us to give them this power that will enable them, under the circumstances detailed in this enactment, to go into the constituencies and prepare their own lists contrary to the existing law, con-tary to the understanding, contrary to what at present is our best and only guarantee, and at the same time they ask us to vote supply, to give them money. The proposition seems to me to be one absolutely untenable and I would not hesitate, fearless of what would be the consequence, to say that I would never consent to such a thing as that. We must follow the very celebrated example of some of our ancestors of old. The Commons of England mustered in the monastery of Westminster, they knew how to close the doors of the refectory and the cloister, shut themselves up and refused to be moved for supply or scutage or aid to the King unless he would come down and cure their grievances, and this they did at the very peril of their lives. We stand in no such peril. Speaker Seymour, I think it was, was committed to the Temple by the King because, speaking in the name of the Commons, he had complained of the cost of the maintenance of the King's mistresses. This is a far more serious grievance, this is a question of the relinquishment unto the government, the giving to the government in its own discretion, of the preparation of the electoral lists and to my mind nothing having any weight whatever has been laid before us to show that this very sweeping change is necessary. Under these circumstances X for one would be faithful to the old principle and I would refuse supply until this grave grievance has been swept away.

I am sorry I had not the opportunity of being in my seat this afternoon when the hon. member for .Tacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) began his speech. I always admire the hon. member when he speaks in the House for his courtesy and for the soundness, as a rule, of his arguments. But this afternoon, in listening to him, I felt that he made certain statements which cannot be borne out by the law as it exists in Quebec. His statement that there is very little or practically no unorganized territory in the province of Quebec, is certainly not borne out by the facts. I have not had occasion to look up the exact extent of the unorganized territory in that province, but I have already cited that in the county of Wright we have 572,397 acres of land. In the county of Pontiac we have 11,577,618 acres of unorganized territory with a population of 1,339 people. I feel that if this Bill will give to the people living in that portion of the province which is unorganized territory the right to vote, then it certainly overcomes a difficulty which we have felt in that province for a very long time and will be an excellent measure of justice to those people.
Has the hon. member read section 17 of the Electoral Act, which provides that the secretary-treasurer of each municipality must prepare the lists of that municipality ?
Is the hon. member quoting from the statute of 1903?
The Act of 1893 as amended up to 1903.

Section 9a of this Bill provides :	.
9a. Notwithstanding anything to the contrary herein contained, voters' lists for the portions of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec which consist of territory not municipally organized and where there is no regular assessment or valuation roll

Those are the words that I would like to point out:
-upon which the voters' lists are based

-&c. The first section which deals with elections in this country and which applies naturally to the province of Quebec is section 6 of the Dominion Elections Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, chapter 6, which reads.
For the purposes of any Dominion election held within the limits of a province, the voters' lists shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be those prepared for the several polling divisions established, 'find which, on the sixtieth day next preceding the day fixed for the nomination of candidates for such Dominion election.
Again section 10 reads.
The qualifications necessary to entitle any person to vote at a Dominion election in any province shall, except as herein otherwise provided, be those established by the laws of that province as necessary to entitle such person to vote in the same part of the province at a provincial election.
Again section 21:
So long as and whenever, for any reason, a certified" copy of any list of voters as finally revised has not been transmitted to or received by the clerk of the Crown in Chancery, pursuant to the provisions of this Act, the original and legal list for Dominion elections shall he the same as that for provincial elections.
Referring to the old law of the province of Quebec to be found In the Revised Statutes of Quebec, the law then practically was, as pointed out by the bon. gentleman:
The secretary-treasurer of each municipality shall, between the first and fifteenth days of the month of September, in each year, make in duplicate, subdivided before each polling subdivision, a list, in alphabetical order, of all persons who, according to the valuation roll

I again point out the word * valuation.'
-then in force in the municipality for municipal purposes, appear to be electors by rea-

son of the immovable property possessed or occupied by them in any manner within the municipality or by reason of being otherwise qualified as set forth in article 9.
There were subsequent amendments to that law and we Und in the statutes of Quebec, 3 Edward VII, chapter 9, this provision :
Section 9. The following persons, and no other, being males, and who, at the time of the deposit of the list under articles 25 and 26 of this Act, are of the full age of twenty-one years, subjects of His Majesty by birth or naturalization and not otherwise legally disqualified, shall be entered upon the list of electors :
1. Owners or occupants, in good faith, of immovable property estimated, according to the valuation roll in force, at a sum of at least three hundred dollars in real value, in any city, municipality entitled to return one or more members to the legislative assembly, or $200 in real value or $20 in annual value in any other municipality.
It goes on to speak of tenants, teachers and so on. Then, we find in this law the meaning of the word ' municipality ' as follows :
The word municipality means every municipality of a parish or part of a parish, of a township or part of a township, or united township, of a village, of a town existing under the operation of the Municipal Code, and every town or city municipality incorporated by charter or special Act.
Now, I see what the hon. member (Mr. Monk) had in mind. He quoted, as I understand, section 32 of the Municipal Code. It is perfectly true that that section brings such unorganized territory under the county council for municipal purposes, but it does not bring it under the county council for the purposes of voting at provincial or federal elections:
The county council may, by a resolution, after public notice to that effect has been duly given, previous to the passing thereof, amd approved and published in the manner prescribed, by article 41, erect into a parish municipality, under the name which belongs to it, according to the rules prescribed, any territory included in one or more townships or part of townships, whether or not erected into municipalities, and which has been constituted into a civil parish, provided that such parish contains a population of three hundred souls and is wholly situated in the county.
I did not quote that section. I quoted section 28.
Yes, that provides for municipal government for municipal purposes, but it does not bring the unorganized territory under the provisions of the statute governing elections.
' Why not?

Because, to begin with, there is no valuation roll upon which the voters' list may be founded.
258J
Does the hon. gentleman pretend that one must be on the valuation roll in order to have his name entered on the electoral list?
The lists are prepared from the valuation roll.

But the hon. gentleman surely knows that the man who earns $300 a year is not entered on the valuation roll, but his name must be put on the voters' list. It has been held, time and again, in our province that it Is not necessary to be on the valuation roll in order to be on the voters' list.

I know that. But my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) is speaking of the preparation of voters' lists. Now, in the general preparation, the voters' list is taken from the valuation roll. My hon. friend has surely mistaken the purpose of section 28 of the Municipal Code. I had not previously looked at that in this argument, but, of course, I knew about It.
I do not think the hon. gentleman has looked very much into this question.
I certainly have had reason to, because I am more affected by it than is the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I have had experience.
I have no doubt that this proposed enactment Is very useful to my hon. friend (Mr. Devlin). [DOT]

It Is very useful because it will bring into existence as voters at the election people who should have the right to vote, but who have no right to vote today. I certainly have not gone to these people to ask them whether they will vote for a Liberal or a Conservative condidate.
I am surprised that my hon. friend has not had them put on the list already. They should be there.
No, I have never put men on the list who had not the right to vote.
You mean, men who would not vote right.

But, going on with the legal argument, I would point out that section 32 provides that unorganized territory may be erected into a municipality provided it has a population of 300 souls and is wholly situated within the county. But, what about the parish that does not contain 300 souls? As a lawyer of the province of Quebec, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk knows it cannot be.
I did not refer to that article, but I quoted the article I did refer to.
The hon. gentleman referred to section 32.
If I did so, it was by mistake.	i	,

Article 32 covers the point the hon. gentleman wanted to make-shows how this territory is brought under the authority of the county council. But I will point out that there is no provision in the law of the province of Quebec to-day which gives the people living in this unorganized territory the right to vote. The hon. gentleman savs it would be only in very remote parts of the province where such cases might be found. I would point out that in the township of Denholme, I think it is, within a very few miles of the city of Ottawa, the residents there, unless they possess property in adjoining parishes municipally erected, have no right to vote. Above the village of Maniwaki or the village of Montcerf, which is only about 117 miles from Ottawa, there is a very large population of farmers who have not the right to vote.
Why not?
Simply' because the law of the province does not allow it, and we have not those the hon. gentleman suggests we should have to put them on the list.
Are they qualified ?
They are property holders and otherwise qualified, but they have not the right to vote.
They must have.
Not under the law.

If my hon. friend will allow me, the Electoral Act specifically imposes upon the secretary-treasurer of the municipality which controls these people the duty of making a list and entering their names in it.
Where does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) find that?

The hon. gentleman quoted from it a few minutes ago-it is section 17, which provides that the secretary-treasurer of each municipality must between the 1st and 15th of September make the list and put upon that list the names of those who, by the assessment roll, have the right to vote, ' or who, by reason of being otherwise qualified, as set forth in article 9 ' and so on -providing for the case exactly where there is no assessment roll.
What particular part of section 9 gives that right?
There is a large enumeration in that article. There are, for instance, those who earn a total of $300 a year-say those who work on the Transcontinental Railway.

Let me read section 17 :
_ The secretary-treasurer of each municipality shall, between the first and fifteenth days of the month of September, in each year, make in duplicate, subdivided for each pol-Mr. MONK.
ling subdivision, a list, in alphabetical order, of all persons who, according to the valuation roll then in force in the municipality for municipal purposes, appear to be electors by reason of the immovable property possessed or occupied by them in any manner within the municipality or by reason of being otherwise qualified as set forth in article 9.
Now I will read to the hon. gentleman article 9, subsection 1 :
Owners or occupants in good faith, or immovable property estimated, according to the valuation roll in force, at a sum of at least three hundred dollars in real value, in any city municipality entitled to return one or more members to the legislative assembly, or two hundred dollars in real value or twenty dollars in annual value in any other municipality.
But if they are not organized municipally how are they going to possess the right?
Read subsection 11.

Persons who are domiciled in the electoral district, and who draw, from their salary or wages, in money or in effects, or from some business, employment, trade or profession, or from some investment, a revenue of at least three hundred dollars per annum, or persons who work by the piece in factories and who derive at least three hundred dollars per annum therefrom.-
Does that cover the son of a farmer who gets a salary from his father on the farm?
What about the $300 a year men?

I am now speaking of farmers in the province of Quebec. We are not providing for transients, people that may pass through a town and that no honest man will attempt to put upon the list. I think the hon. gentleman ought to be satisfied by this time that there is a large portion of the population in the province of Quebec who have, under the existing law, no right to vote at a Dominion election. But by section 9a of this Bill these people will have a right to vote and therefore justice will he done to them. I have no hesitation in saying that this Bill will meet with the universal approval of the people of the province of Quebec, and that it will cover a long felt want. The only reason I have heard hon. gentlemen adduce against this Bill is the fear that they may have dishonest officials to operate it. That is a very foolish argument. If every time we wished to pass a law in this House we were deterred bv the fear that it would not be efficiently enforced, or. that some dishonest officials might put it into operation, why, we would pass no law whatever in this House. When I first glanced at this Bill I immediately thought of the poor people residing in the county which I represent, people who have said to me time and again: It is a shame that your parliament does

not pass a law which will give us the right to vote. Merchants have come to me, farmers have come to me and have asked why their names should not be put upon the voters' list.
Has the hon. gentleman ever appealed to the legislature of Quebec to remedy that defect he complains of?
I leave to the legislature of Quebec to deal with matters coming within the sphere of their jurisdiction. At the present time I am considering what laws this House is called upon to pass.
Does this Bill propose to fix a basis of representation ?
No, but this Bill will bring into force in unorganized territories the xjrovisions of the law as they exist in organized territories.
If this Bill becomes law will it empower you to place on the revised list any man anywhere who has not, under the province in which he lives already, the property qualification for a voter?
Speaking for the province of Quebec, provided he has under the provincial law the necessary qualifications of an elector, and tnose qualifications are laid down in section 9.
If he has those necessary qualifications now?
But he has not. [DOT]
This Bill does not propose to amend the qualification.
Not at all.
Then how will he have the right to vote under this Bill?

Because this Bill will bring him under the operation of section 9a I have just read.
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary herein contained, voters' lists for the portions of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec which consist of territory not municipally organized and where there is no regular assessment or valuation roll upon which voters' lits are based.
The moment a man lives in unorganized territory he has at present no right to vote, but the moment we pass this Bill then he will be brought under the operation of the provisions as. we have them to-day. As the Minister of Justice remarks, the new lists which will be prepared under this Bill will be prepared according to the laws of the province as they now exist, and, therefore people who have the necessary qualifications to vote in organized territory will then have the right to vote in unorganized territory. That is the whole point. Therefore, I have no hesitation in saying that I
will give this Bill my entire support. I cannot speak with any personal knowledge of the operation of the election laws in the province of Manitoba, but I have no hesitation in saying from a study of the Bill and from what I have heard in this House that this Bill is going to cover a great many irregularities. Surely the people of Manitoba are not as dishonest as hon. gentlemen opposite wish to make them out. Surely if hon. gentlemen opposite have had amongst their organizers certain dishonest people who have given wrong affidavits or who have taken from the proper, authorities the seal of the court and placed it in their headquarters, if hon. gentlemen have had that experience with their organizers, there is no reason to suppose that if Jhey come into the Liberal camp they will not find men who are prepared to act honestly and to put this law into proper execution.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to name some of the irregularities in the Manitoba Election Act?
I am speaking, not of irregularities in the law itself, but in the operation of the law.
Some of Mr. Leach's work possibly.
No, I was referring to some of the affidavits that were fraudulently obtained, according to newspaper reports.

Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Is there a provision in this Act that an enumerator can take it upon himself to be the assessor of property in unorganized territory in the province of Quebec, so as to put values on farms in order to find out whether the owners are qualified to vote in that province?

We have a provision which gives a man the right to vote according to valuation. The hon. gentleman's objection is well taken, but it has no basis in fact, because the municipal councils, under the working of the provincial Act, will find out what is the valuation of that property before the owner is allowed to vote. There will be absolutely no difficulty on that score. I have no hesitation in giving my cordial support to this Bill, as I believe it is one of the best ever submitted to this House.

Mr. Speaker, I am not a lawyer but the arguments which have been advanced by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat seem to me to have been most extraordinarily mixed-so much so that I could not help coming to the conclusion that he must have a very poor notion of the pro-J visions of this measure. .Of the two argu-

ments which have been advanced from the province of Quebec up to the present, I could certainly have no hesitation whatever in giving the preference to that submitted by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).
'Mr. DEVLIN. If I were in your place, I would have no hesitation either.

I am aware of that, but I am not speaking from a party point or view. I am speaking from the point of view of clearness, and I should certainly say that in that respect the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has been a lamentable failure. Let me call attention first of all to the fact that there has not been one argument put forward so far to justify the application of this measure to the province of British Columbia. We have not had a British Columbian declare that the working of the Dominion election law in that province is unsatisfactory, and that such a radical alteration in the law of the Dominion is required as regards that province. The only reason, it seems to me, which has induced the government to apply this Bill to that province is that the administration of the provincial law with regard to elections is honest and satisfactory and that is what this government is anxious to avoid.

Admitting for the sake of argument that we have an honest voters' list in British Columbia, does my hon. friend pretend that when that list is not adapted for federal purposes we should not pass a law to adapt it for those purposes ?
No argument has been laid before the House to show that it is not adapted for federal purposes and no complaints have been raised.

Surely my hon. friend is aware, if he knows anything about the lists in British Columbia, that in several instances provincial districts and federal districts do not coincide and consequently the lists are not adapted for federal purposes.

I am willing to admit that I know but little about the law of British Columbia, but what I say is that we have not heard any member from that province argue that there is any reason or necessity for auy change. If there were no other circumstances, those in which the Bill was introduced are sufficient to create grave suspicion as to the honesty of the government. This measure is one which is bound to have most far-reaching effects. It is perhaps the most important Bill with regard to elections which has ever been brought before the people. It changes our election law in three important particulars, In this short Bill of eight pages, we find three great principals embodied. First, a complete abandonment of the secrecy of the 'ballot. That is a matter which de-Mr. LAKE
serves a Bill for itself and the long and earnest consideration of this House. The second is the abandonment of the principle of provincial franchises, which was adopted by this House, after very long and careful discussion, some years ago.] Third, iit adopts the principle that a company or an association incorporated for political purposes may collect and distribute without restriction an election fund of any size and thus evade all the provisions with regard to individuals. This is the Bill which was promised in the speech from the Throne at the opening of this session. The government allowed four or five months of this session to pass before bringing it down. The ordinary explanation of this delay would be that the government had been spending a great part of that time in considering the details ; but if we are to believe the Minister of Justice, that was not the case at all. According to him, its chief provisions were put on paper some four or five months before the beginning of the session and had then received the consideration of the government. Let me recall to the House words he used in moving the first reading, after we had been in session some four or five mouths. He said:
The measure I am now introducing is one I committed to paper some four or five months before the present session, and with the exception of one or two details which re-maioed for further consideration, these provinces had therefore that consideration at my hands and the hands of the government.
It would therefore seem that the government has decided upon the details of this Bill, except in one or two minor points, months and months ago and yet they wait until near the close of the session, when the members are weary with their parliamentary duties, to place this important measure before the House. The Minister of Justice explained some unimportant details of the Bill and then proceeded to say :
The other amendments in this Bill "are of possibly minor character altogether.
But let us see what the Minister of Justice describes as being of a minor character. First of all there is this section 1 which the Minister of Justice himself now admits to be the main feature of the measure. He was speaking of that which occurred in Manitoba last election when large numbers of persons had been disfranchised by the thin red line outrage, and he said :
I am confident that the omission of such names were few in number and that there was nothing of intentional wrong-doing. However that may be, it is of interest that provision should be made in the Elections Act which will authorize and permit the officers of the law to make that redistribution of names.
That is all he said about that matter, and he goes on to explain why he considers even that necessary :

A riding for Dominion purposes may contain portions of a dozen different polling subdivisions established for provincial purposes and the officials conducting the Dominion elections, have of necessity to transcribe from the general list to a special list for the purpose 6f that poll, the names of the voters who properly ought to be assigned to the particular poll. I am proposing, in 'the Bill I have prepared, a clause which will authorize that to be done.
That is all the explanation that was given by the Minister of Justice of this most important portion of the Bill, this portion of the Bill which completely abrogates the adoption of the provincial franchise In so far as it relates to two great provinces. This want of candour, this want of honesty in the explanation of the Bill by the Minister of Justice, makes one naturally very suspicions of the intentions of the government in introducing such a measure. Another of these minor details which the Minister of Justice referred to Involves the secrecy of the ballot and. this is what he said about it:
I do not seek to conceal from the House the fact that to remedy this, to permit such numbered ballot or ballots containing marks of identification to be counted, is a radical departure from the whole principle of the Dominion Elections Act. It has been said liy learned judges, and no. doubt correctly said, that tlie ruling principle of the Dominion Elections Act is secrecy at all costs, secrecy even at the cost of defeating the will of the people by preventing the counting of ballots which are perfectly good when they leave the hands of the electors, but which may afterwards be vitiated by the deputy returning officer or some other officials. If it is a question whether that over-riding principle of secrecy is or is not to be encroacbed upon foi the sake of preserving the individual vote and securing a true expression of the will of the voter and of the people, then, in my judgment, the principle of secrecy ought to give way, and not the principle of giving to the voter the means of expressing his true wish at the polls and carrying out that wish in the counting of the ballots.
How could any intelligent man say that this was a minor detail of this franchise Bill ? Now, in addition to this want of candour of the Minister of Justice when he introduced the Bill, it has occurred to me that when he moved the second reading he made statements which were calculated to mislead the House and which were only partially the truth. Speaking of the thin red line outrage he said it was the returning officers who had used the thin red line, but every member of the House must have known perfectly well that that statement was a suppression of the whole truth, and that in most cases these alterations on the voters' lists were made by Mr. Leach, the organizer of the Liberal party in Manitoba. Again, the Minister of Justice^ stated that these alterations were authorized by the provincial law, only, that a black line was
to be used, and he said that these alterations were made by officials of the provincial government, keeping back the fact that the authorization in the provincial law is only given to judges who are of course officers of the federal government. In other particulars I noticed time and again that the Minister of Justice was suppressing the true facts and was not candid with the House. Nothing could be more calculated to arouse suspicion than the statements made by that hon. gentleman both on the first reading and the second reading of the Bill. Now, the very first feature of this Bill involves a departure from the principle of adopting provincial lists for Dominion elections. I have frequently been asked on the public platform if this government had not failed to carry out all the promises it made the people before it came to power, and I have always answered that the only one promise they kept was the adoption of the provincial franchise. I regret to say that I shall have to abandon even that moderate praise for the government as to carrying out Its preelection promises, for it seems that now they have abandoned that pledge with all the rest.	.
All of the arguments which were made by the Minister of Justice in urging that the first clause of this Bill should be adopted were directed to the necessity for a proper and thorough revision of the lists drawn up by the provincial authorities, on the ground that no opportunity was given for such revision ; and yet we find that the provision he is making is simply for the drawing up of lists by the officials of this government, and for no revision whatever, either by the officials this government may appoint or by the judges who should be appointed under the provincial law. The Bill states that after the writs of election have been issued the government shall have the lists prepared, and, as my hon. friend from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) pointed out, the time occupied in carrying out the provision of the provincial Act is so long that it would make it absolutely impossible in almost every case for any revision of these lists to take place. So that the Minister of Justice could not have been sincere in arguing that there was a necessity for the revision of the provincial lists. What he desires, and what hon. gentlemen opposite desire, is simply that they shall draw up their own lists subject to no revision whatever, and, in drawing up improper lists, shall be in a position to capture the country at the next general election.
The hon. Minister of Justice spoke of the administration and preparation of the lists by the provincial authorities as being an engine of tyranny and oppression. To my mind there has been nothing whatever proved in this House against the honourable, careful manner in which the provincial lists in the province of Manitoba have been prepared. Bat I think we had very full

and very complete proof of the tyranny and oppression which we are to expect from the officials of this government, if they are to draw up these lists, in the speech delivered here the other day by the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce), who showed the abominable manner in which an attempt had been made to steal his constituency from him at the last election by stuffing the list with the names of persons who had never existed or had left the country or had died before the list was drawn up. To the charge that there has been tyranny and oppression in the preparation and administration of the lists in Manitoba, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. W. J. Roche) gave a most exhaustive reply last night. To my mind that reply was absolutely unanswerable ; it has not been answered yet, and I do not believe any attempt will be made to answer it. ' For everv statement he made he gave chapter and text, and I am convinced that the Prime Minister sitting in his seat in the House, was more than half persuaded that he had been forced into a most improper measure by false representations on the part fo his followers.' What evidence has been offered to us on the other side of fraud and oppression? We have had assertions, but the only proof we have had has been innumerable extracts from newspapers, mostly from the Manitoba ' Free Press,' which we nil know is a paper with an extreme party bin*, which receives an enormous amount of pecuniary assistance every year from this government. Let me instance the case of the hon. member for Ins-gar (Mr. Greenway), who stood up in this House with a list in his hand and told us that he had lived for nearly thirty years in his present constituency, that he knew almost every man in it. and that he was prepared to say that there were a large number of names on that list which should not be there, and that a number of names had been omitted from it which should be there. He was promptly challenged to mention a name on the list that should not be there. He stated that he could give the names in his own neighbourhood, and that he would write them down and send them to the leader of the opposition if he so desired ; but the fact remains that after making the boast that he did. he was not able to mention one name when called upon to to do. Then we had the proofs uttered by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Bole), who went sponsor for the affidayits of criminals, which were drawn up nearly a year ago, and which, although there has been a session of the legislature of Manitoba since, and although those affidavits had reference entirely to the provincial elections in Manitoba, had never yet been placed before the public or been mentioned in the Manitoba legislature. No member of that House had the hardihood to stand as godfather of such an extraordinary lot of < Mr. LAKE.
misstatements as were contained in those affidavits. I believe that the telegram which the hon. member for Marquette read in reference to those affidavits has absolutely discredited them, and has put the government in a very bad position indeed. 1 do not know that I have ever read of a more discreditable incident than the reading those affidavits before this House, in view of the fact that they had been purchased from a criminal wlio is even now a refugee from justice.
In the earlier part of this debate it was charged that the members of the opposition had nothing more to say in regard to the thin red line outrage, that there was nothing in it, and that we had got tired of repeating it. I think the government must be enirely without shame in regard to elections in this country, and I was not surprised to hear my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) call attention to the astounding nature of the facts which had been brought out in regard to tlie thin red line outrage in Manitoba, and yet members oil tlie other side of tlie House seem to think nothing of it. They think it is a perfectly natural and proper thing to appoint returning officers who have so little regard for tlie duties of their office that they will hand over the lists to the organizer of one political partv and allow him to mutilate them as he will.
How could the hon. gentleman arrange those lists without a repetition of the thin red line episode in some form or other ?
The law provides that tlie returning officer himself shall make those changes. That has been already pointed out.
Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to point out again ?

If tlie bon. gentleman likes to wait, I will look it up. but it has been pointed out over and over again in this House, as lie knows perfectly well. He thought he would put up a bluff that I had not looked into the election law.
I do no know what the hon. gentleman means by bluff.

If the hon. gentleman considers his own character, he will have a pretty good idea of it. Returning officers should be men pf high standing. It sepms to me that since this government have been in power they have considered the appointment of returning officer to be a matter of political patronage ; they have certainly used it as such in my part of the world. That is certainly one office which should be entirely removed from political patronage, that of the man who has to stand between the two great parties of this country and see that there is fair-play between them. There is no provision whatever in this Bill

for a penalty upon any returning officer who is so recreant to his duty as to do what was done by the Manitoba returning officers, who handed over the lists to an organizer of one of the great political parties.
The test case which was taken in the matter in the district of Provencher showed the extraordinary way in which the returning officer worked in with one of the political parties. It showed that the poll books were stored in the Liberal committee rooms. It showed also that aftr they were collected they were again placed in the Liberal committee rooms. Is that any ,,iacc for ballot boxes before or after an exciting election, to be manipulated, handled or tampered with? I ask the Prime Minister if he considers that a right or proper thing. In my own constituency the Liberal committee room was in the same building as the office of the returning officer, one was on the upper floor and the other on the lower floor, and after the election the ballot boxes were all stored in the Liberal committee rooms. I know that, as people could see them through the windows. Further than that, I know that the election clerk who, as the right hon. gentleman knows, acts for the returning officer in certain questions, was content with holding that one office of election clerk, but also held office as secretary of the Central Liberal committee. I myself have in my possession a letter which he addressed on the day before the election to one of the deputy returning officers telling him he was to accept the votes of certain threshers who were working in that vicinity and signing himself 'Secretary Central Committee.' The ease is perfectly clear, here is a man supposed to have some authority with the returning officers writing to them the day before the election, telling them what voters they were to accept and what voters not to accept. I consider there should be some provision for a severe penalty upon an election official who behaves in a pariioan manner and who does not withdraw himself from all communication with one party or the other.
In reference to the thin red line scandal let me point out that after one of the constituencies had been stolen from the Conservative party and a Liberal had been elected by means of the outrage perpetrated by R. E. A. Leach, the organizer of the Lib

"*al party, he and others who acted with k' * in this matter were rewarded for winning it seat for the government by being appoint to seats under the Dominion government. I. mch himself was appointed inspector of la: 1 agencies in the Northwest. This I consider vas simply an outrage on public decency when you consider all the talk there was over the illegal way in which Leach had manipulated these lists, thereby changing the results of the elections. I believe it is intended to encourage the corruption, I cannot see it in any other way. I believe that if persons who were corrupt in these elections in the interests of the Liberal party are to be rewarded by this government for such acts, we shall find many others who are ready to be similarly corrupt expecting like rewards. Let me say the appointment of the man who does these things to a position in the civil service is in itself an inducement to corruption in the civil service, and it certainly is a direct inducement to civil servants to take part in elections in spite of the fact that this House has declared that a civil servant shall not take part in elections either Dominion or local. All the debates in regard to the Interior Department at any rate, which have taken place in the House for the last session or two, have gone to show that no punishment will be meted out to officials of that department if they do take part in elections. In fact, I will go further and say that the statements of the minister of that department have always been more or less of an incentive to officials to help on his own party in the elections.
In regard to Mr. Leach's appointment as head of the Land Department of the Department of the Interior in the Northwest, let me read a letter from a gentleman who was a supporter of hon. gentlemen opposite in the old days, who was a member of the Liberal party when he wrote this letter, although at the time he did not agree with them as to their treatment of the Liberals in the west and ran as a candidate for the provincial rights party, still calling himself a Liberal. I refer to Mr. R. L. Chisholm, who ran for the district of Battleford. Mr. Chisholm wrote:
lit is true that never before was the civil service machinery employed so extensively in this western country ias during this last contest. Some officials practically abandoned their official duties during the last few weeks and worked very hard against us, particularly perhaps in this constituency. It has always been known that the civil service exerts an overpowering influence in this locality. In this contest the service, almost to a man, was disposed to stand back and see an even fight between my opponent and myself. Some were disposed at first to help me.
Mr. Chisholm had been an official iu that office and naturally his brother officials were ratherTriendly with him than the reverse.

Leach made two or three trips here at brief intervals, and Talbot came frequently and a man named Perry, an organizer, w'ho gets credit for our northern polls outrages, came several times, and the servants fell in one by one until at the finish they were working a~ they never did before. I feel a little reluctance in formulating specific charges against the civil servants here because I know that each and every one who went into the battle against me was pushed in much against his inclination and under various forms of duress.

Further on he says in reference to Leach:
I am satisfied that he is the individual that we may thank for nearly all the activity of his fellow servants here and to a large extent elsewhere in the province. I have it on very good authority that Leach is now persecuting the agent of Dominion lands here because the latter refused to act as a party tool. The agent of Dominion lands will not discuss the matter at all.
That shows how Leach immediately got to work for the party as soon as he was put in a position to do so as a reward for his services in regard to the lists in Manitoba.

Nobody, of course, will challenge the statements made, but I think it is only fair to state that the reason the statements are not questioned is that the gentleman who wrote that letter is dead. Of course we will not question the statements under the circumstances.
I am not sure but I think I had this on record before Mr. Chisholm died. I am very sorry that Mr. Chisholm, who was a most estimable gentleman, unfortunately died since that time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Might I say a word in regard to the persecution of the land agent at Battleford because of his lack of partisanship in that election? It might interest the House to know that he has been persecuted by having his salary raised since that time.

This gentleman, as I have said, is a candidate of the Liberal party, and, at that time, always called himself a good Liberal :
In many cases they held ont as bribes the patent to a homestead, and in some oases the bribe was paid.
With all the authority that that gentleman possesses, he made that statement.
In others it was never handed over. He knew of many instances in the Souris electoral district where the government homestead inspector held out concessions as a bribe to some electors.
Mr. Scott. You are aware of the statement made bv the Hon. Frank Oliver that officials are liable to' dismissal if they are reported.
Mr. Brown bad read the statement of the Minister of the Interior, and he expected that Mr. Oliver would be given a chance to make good Ms promise in that respect. It was only by the Minister of the Interior taking the matter up that the desired results would be attained.
Mr. Brown had read the statement of the Minister of the Interior and expected that that hon. gentleman would be given a chance to make good his promise.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lake) what he is reading from ?
From the report of the proceedings of the Legislative Assembly.
An official or a newspaper report ?

When I was in the assembly no official report was taken. This is the report which appeared in two local newspapers-or, later, three-and nasted in a book and considered a ' Hansard ' of the proceedings. I do not think that the method has been changed since, although I have often wished to get a full account of the proceedings.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lake) has misunderstood. From which newspaper is he quoting ?

I am not quite certain, but I think it is the Regina ' Sun.' I may add that I have had the list of officials who were working in Mr. Brown's constituency, with some statements in connection with the constituency which Mr. Brown contested at that time. I was given names of the officials but, in addition to that, I was able to lay before the House, almost immediately after the statement was made by Mr. Brown, a number of affidavits-nine or ten, I think-proving that officials of the Department of the Interior had acted as scrutineers and in other partisan ways in the elections that had just taken place. The Minister of the Interior had the opportunity, as Mr. Brown suggested, of making good what he had said, but I have yet to hear of one single dismissal of an official for taking

part in these elections and breaking the rule which had been laid down in this House against officials taking an active partisan part in the elections of members for the provincial House. I have another letter, which I shall not be able to read, from another Liberal, who was a candidate of the provincial rights party in that election. He says the same thing as the others regarding the officials in his district, and the Minister of the Interior knows that we placed ease after case before him and he refused to take action. He himself has appeared on the platfoiim with an official of his department acting, as chairman in addressing a party political meeting.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Pernaps I may be allowed to explain, in order to prevent misapprehension of the case. The person alluded to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lake) was a subland agent. And I would like to say, as I said before-and I have always taken the same position-that, inasmuch as we do not pay the sub-land agent for the whole of his time, nor do we pay him enough salary to give him a living-and do not pretend to ; we only pay him part of his living-in the other part of his time he is as free to exercise his political rights as if we did not pay for any part of his time.

That is the explanation the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) gives. But let me point out that this man had a regular monthly salary, $30 a month at that time. The minister knows that such an official exercises a most powerful influence in that country as being the sub-agent of the department and this gives him a considerable amount of patronage as well. I do not think it wnatters whether an official is high-paid or low-paid ; he is an official of the whole country and is paid by the people of both political parties. The government has no right to use him for party purposes and for the advancement of the interests of one narty over that of the other. I do not care if he only receives $5 a month, the position is the same; the government has no right to use him for party work as it has done practically with so many. The sub-land agents in the Northwest often get a larger salary than $30 a month. In several of the cases that were brought to the attention of the minister, the salary was ample to remunerate the official for the whole of his titme ; yet, as I said, I do not think the minister has taken action in any case.
