I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lake); but I would like your ruling on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I think the hon. gentleman has wandered from the motion before you in his discussion of the resolutino to which he has referred, of the cases of sub-land
agents, and so on. I submit that this is not properly within the scope of a discussion on a motion for the second reading.

I am pointing out that there should be a provision in this Bill to prevent civil servants from taking part in elections. We have referred to the fact that there are omissions in the Bill. This is a Bill for the amendment of the Elections Act, and' this was promised to the country ever so long ago, and I consider it perfectly in order that I should discuss such an amendment as this. I was working up to that point that, although this House has decided by resolution that officials should not take part in elections, yet, when the government bring in an Election Bill they will not put that into the Bill, and this shows simply that the government do not intend to have that carried out.
Are you in favour of disfranchising civil servants ?

No, but I am not in favour of permitting them to take an active part in elections.
Mr. e. m. Macdonald, how would you do that ?

Certainly I would not dis-rrancnise civil servants. I nave seen a
little of the working of the Civil Service Act in the old country. Usually men enter the service at a pretty early age, they can enter from the age of sixteen upwards. I myself was a little more than sixteen when I entered the civil service, and one of the first things I was told was that while I had the privilege of exercising the right to vote, I must carefully abstain from active partisan work. That is the only way in which you can get a really good civil service in this country. The way in which pressure has been put upon civil servants in this country to induce them to take an active [DOT]part in elections puts them in a very awkward position. One thing the government should provide in their proposed Civil Service Act is to make it absolutely clear that while the civil servant may exercise his right to vote as the expression of an individual opinion, he must not exert any political influence. To my mind this Election Bill should provide severe penalties against any man who is in the pay of the Dominion government, canvassing, addressing meetings, acting as scrutineer, or taking an active part in any other way in Dominion elections. The right hon. leader of this government has laid down the principle in forcible language that there should be no interference by civil servants either in provincial or Dominion elections. While I am upon that point, let me call his attention to the opinion of Mr. Mackenzie in regard to this question. In 1873, Mr. Mackenzie placed this resolution on the Order Paper.
81(53

That it is highly criminal in any minister or ministers or other servants under the Crown, directly or indirectly, to use the powers of office in the election of representatives to serve in parliament, and any attempt at such influence will at all times be resented by this House as aimed at its own dignity, honour and independence.
Let me submit that expression of opinion of one of the first men in this country, a man whose memory is held in the highest respect by both parties, let ime submit it as worthy of adoption. Let me urge the government to put into force the principle which this House has adopted, that civil servants shall be punished who take an active part In elections.
Another matter which I have already referred to as being one of supreme importance is the abolition of the secrecy of the ballot which is involved in the Bill before the House. I read the statement of the Minister of Justice in regard to that provision. He says clearly that this measure does away with the secrecy of the ballot, and that where it comes to be a question, by the inadvertence of the returning officer in placing a mark upon the ballot, whether the ballot should be rejected or counted, it is better to have it counted. This provision means then, as pointed out by the leader of the opposition, that every ballot may he legally numbered, and that the natme of the voter may he placed upon the back of it by the returning officer. Therefore every ballot which is cast in the coming elections may be legally marked by the deputy returning officer, and every voter may be identified. It seems to me that nothing should so disturb the old Liberals of this country as a sign of degeneracy in the present Liberal party, and that the government, without any compunction, introduce an amendment which does away with what used to be one of the great principles of Lib-eralisim, the secrecy of the ballot. This measure is one providing for open voting, and there are many people in this country who believe that open voting is the better system, that it is right and proper that a man should go up to the poll in a manly way and mark his vote in the open. This measure does not provide for open voting, but it does provide that the deputy returning officer may make a mark on the ballot so that he may tell how every man votes. Of course the object of this provision is clear enough to every member of this House, but I think it is a change that the people will resent as an infringement upon their privilege of voting for whom they like. They claim the privilege of voting without any pressure being placed upon them by their employers or others upon whom they are dependent. I mistake very much the opinion of the honest people in the Northwest if they do not resent in the most vigorous tnanner this invasion of their rights. Large numbers of people Mr. LAKE.
are coming into the country from abroad, and are becoming citizens of Canada, and it will be possible, under this new provision, to put pressure upon them to vote for the government candidate. In many instances these people are dependent upon the good-will of government officials in the matter of homesteading. In this connection I would like to mention a circumstance that came to my notice the other day. An officer of this government who took an active part in the election in Prince Albert had to flee the country for having been guilty of a criminal act in holding bogus polls and making bogus voters' lists. He and two others had to flee from justice into the Uuited States, and one of the three who was not an official at the time but who fled into the United States, was a homesteader, and this government gave him an extension of time while he was residing in the United States in order that no one else should co'me in and cancel his homestead. Is it not an outrage that a fugitive from justice should be allowed an extension of time in which to perform his residence duties, simply because he was fleeing from justice after having committed this outrage in the provincial elections which were being held ? Furthermore, with regard to this matter of the marked ballots, iet me point out how it will affect those cases in which bribery is being practised. We have seen the evidence in connection with the London election trial and other trials. We are seeing the expense and trouble that the Liberal organizers are put to in getting fcnen to instruct deputy returning officers how to mutilate the ballots and how to have them marked so that they can be identified. And this provision of the Bill seems devised to save the Liberal party any further expense in this connection and to enable the deputy returning officers to know how every man voted so as to ensure that those who* had been bribed delivered the goods.
The hon. member for Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) said a few words the other day on this subject. He glossed it over. All you would have to do, he said, is to provide a penalty for the retruning officer who would he guilty of such practices. But what struck me was how significant it was that the Minister of Justice should have inserted this provision without at the sa'.ne time providing a severe penalty for the returning officer who would mark ballots so that they could he identified. Either the hon. minister, was careless or else it was his intention to facilitate the marking of these ballots. I think it would have been very much better if, instead of providing for the marking of ballots .by the deputy returning officer, he should have provided a penalty to be inflicted upon those who wilfully marked ballots in that way, and thus put a stop to some of the briber^ and corruption which is now being practised.

I do not intend to discuss at length the extraordinary provision which legalizes corruption by a company incorporated for party purposes. That provision and all the other provisions of this measure will no doubt be most thoroughly discussed in committee and we then hope to have some sweeping amendments accepted. But what occurs to me as perfectly evident is that if we accept this clause as it stands, it will allow any company to commit any of those acts of corruption which are severely forbidden to individuals.
As I said a short time ago when the First Minister was not in his seat, in my opinion the right lion, gentleman was almost persuaded by the cogent and eloquent arguments put forward by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) last night. I believe that in his heart, my right hon. friend knows that my hon. friend from Marquette was justified in the statements he made. My hon. friend (Mr. Roche) certainly proved every statement by chapter and text. I believe that the right hon. gentleman was convinced last night that the Manitoba law is fair, equitable, and just, and that he has not been truly informed as to it by the hon. gentlemen from that province who sit behind him.
What struck me just now when my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was speaking, is, that he was perfectly willing to allow the provisions of the existing law with regard to the province of Quebec to stand as they were. He had no complaint whatever and yet the province of Quebec is in the hands of the Liberal party. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) had no objection to that, but on the other hand we find that the main reason to allowing the lists to be drawn up by the provincial authorities in Manitoba and British Columbia is the fact that the local governments of these provinces are in the hands of the opponents of the Dominion government. But we have had no suggestion made that there is anything wrong with the lists in British Columbia. I do not think that the right hon. gentleman realizes the bitterness of the feeling which exists in certain parts of this country with regard to the provisions of this Bill. Should this Bill go through, I would warn him that the people who are deprived of this most sacred right of the franchise by wholesale are likely to take the law into their own hands and commit illegal acts.
Will my hon. friend find out one clause in the Act which deprived anybody of his franchise?

Of course there is no clause which directly deprives anybody of his franchise, but it has been clearly proved by my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Boyce) that it is quite possible people will be deprived of the franchise by the thousand. In my opinion, should this clause be carried into effect, that is bound to happen. Even if the officials appointed by the government desire to be honest, they have only a short time between the issue of a wyit for the election and the election itself, to draw up all those lists, and under the Manitoba Act it would be impossible to have the lists revised. So that even if the officials desired to be honest, there can be no guarantee of their having proper lists. And further, we may expect that some dishonest men will be appointed to prepare those lists, and we shall then find people deprived of their franchise, which will cause intense bitterness of feeling. We bad the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) pointing out last night that in the polling division of Beausejour, a certain number of men, who had been deprived by this thin red line outrage of their votes, entered the polls and threatened to destroy the ballot boxes. I can well imagine people from the old country, where no such interference with the rights of the electorate would be tolerated, being strongly inclined to make trouble when such outrages are committed.
The right hon. gentleman who leads this House and who holds the fate of this Bill in the hollow of his hand, will himself be personally responsible to a very large extent if this Bill goes through in its present form, if there should be such unfortunate occurrences as I have mentioned or if there should be bloodshed. After all the Prime Minister is the principal beneficiary if this Bill works out as I believe it will, to return his party to power, and he is the man who should be held mainly responsible for it. I appeal to him.' He has held a foremost position in this great country of Canada for the last twelve years; he has held a foremost position before the whole world. Is he going to stultify the last few years of his prime ministership by allowing legislation to pass which in British Columbia, Manitoba and the unorganized territories of Ontario and Quebec is a violation of the principles with regard to the franchise which prevail in the other parts of Canada? Is the right hon. gentleman going to stultify his great record-for he has a record-by countenancing such an outrage? I believe the people of this country have changed their mind about the right hon. gentleman and that they will not continue him in power, but is he going to let it be said that one of the last acts of his administration was the doing away with the secrecy of the ballot? I don't believe the Prime Minister will allow such a thing to take place. I believe he will look to his future reputation and that he will step in and withdraw the obnoxious clauses of this Bill.
